Game of Life (Conway & Gardener, 1970s)

SETUP

  • Infinite checkerboard (2D) of patches where each patch is either alive (green) or dead (dark blue)

GO

  • Each cell looks at its Moore neighborhood (8)
    • If I have fewer than two live neighbors, I die.
    • If I have exactly two live neighbors, I stay unchanged.
    • If I have exactly three live neighbors, I become (or stay) alive.
    • If I have more than three live neighbors, I die.

Game of Life in NetLogo (Us, 2026)

  ; patches update their status
  ask patches [
    if live-neighbors = 3 [ set pcolor green ]  ; comfortable neighborhood - live cells born
    if live-neighbors < 2 [ set pcolor blue ]   ; isolated patches die
    if live-neighbors > 3 [ set pcolor blue ]   ; overcrowded patches die
  ]

Emergent Patterns

  • Still Lifes (e.g., A 4 cell block-shape)​
  • Oscillator patterns repeat over time. (e.g., a blinker)​
  • Spaceships, some Life shapes can move across the Life world. (e.g., glider)​

Universe as a Cellular Automata

  • Konrad Zuse (1969) – Calculating Space​
  • Ed Fredkin (1990) – “We hypothesize that there will be found a single CA rule that models all of microscopic physics; ​and models it exactly.”​
  • Stephen Wolfram – Classified all 1D CA​

Might seem absurd, but it has been defended​:

Zuse - universe is discrete, not continuous and is in fact a large CA​ Fredkin – digital mechanics​ Wolfram – physics prodigy and software entrepreneur, inventor of Mathematica, 256 possible rules for 1D CA (2^8)​ Matthew Cook proved some of the rules are Turing complete, universal computers​

CA are discrete, but we think of the world as continuous we have modeled it as continuous as it is easier for our math​. But when we drill down, we see atoms and particles, not continuum​. Max speed in universe, but in CA, you get a maximum speed due to the layout of cells and the ticking of the clock​. Wolfram has massive book: A New Kind of Science, hundreds of examples from bio and physics world generated by CA​ ​ Difference between CAs and ABMs, less parsimonious, so to some less elegant, but though CAs are universal, they can be very slow, imagine trying to to do a social simulation with a CA where you have to keep the people together just like we did with gliders.​

NetLogo Syntax Specifics

Primitive Types

Two basic types of primitives:

  • Commands: change things in the world (function with no return value)
  • Reporters: give you information about stuff (function with a return value)

Examples!

Commands

  • forward (fd)
  • right (rt)
  • create-turtles (crt)
  • set
  • ask
  • show

Reporters

  • heading
  • color
  • random
  • one-of
  • turtles
  • length

Student Presentation

Heroes and Cowards

  • A game played at various Complex Systems conferences

SETUP

  • People spread out in a room
  • Each person is assigned as a hero or a coward
  • Each person picks one other person (in their head) to be their friend and one to be their enemy

GO

  • If you are a hero, move toward the midpoint between your friend and enemy
  • If you are a coward, move toward the spot behind your friend relative to your enemy

Movement Behaviors

Heroic Movement

  • Move toward the midpoint between your friend and enemy

Cowardly Movement

  • Move toward the spot behind your friend relative to your enemy

More formalized Agent Rules

SETUP

  • Create NUMBER turtles at random locations
    • If PERSONALITIES is “hero”, color I’m blue
    • If PERSONALITIES is “coward”, color I’m yellow
    • If PERSONALITIES is "mixed", flip a coin.
    • I pick one other turtle as a friend
    • I pick one other turtle as an enemy

GO (at each tick)

  • Each turtle asks itself:
    • If I’m blue, I act heroically
    • If I’m yellow, I’ll act cowardly
